analysis.one_liner: Penalizes companies that misclassify employees as independent contractors and requires written notice of workers' classification.
analysis.headline: The Senate labor committee held one hearing on the bill but never voted on it, and it died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required companies to keep records on everyone who works for them as a contractor, and to give every worker a written notice stating whether they are classified as an employee or an independent contractor. It would have made misclassification itself a violation of wage law, doubled the damages owed to workers shorted on wages or overtime when they were misclassified, and added civil penalties up to $5,000 per worker for repeat or willful violators. It also would have pushed states to audit employers who misclassify workers to dodge unemployment insurance taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers treated as independent contractors when they function as employees. Misclassification costs them minimum wage and overtime protections, employer payroll taxes, and unemployment insurance coverage. The bill's recordkeeping requirement, written notice, and legal presumption that an undocumented worker is an employee unless the company proves otherwise would make it far easier for them to claim back wages.

how_it_helps.text: Requires companies to give every worker written notice of whether they are classified as an employee or a non-employee, with information on their rights and how to contact the Department of Labor [S2][S3].

Makes failing to accurately classify a worker a violation of the Fair Labor Standards Act, and doubles liquidated damages for minimum wage and overtime violations when the employer also misclassified the worker [S2][S3].

Creates a legal presumption that a worker is an employee unless the employer kept the required records and gave the required notice, and the employer must rebut it with clear and convincing evidence [S3].
Adds civil penalties of up to $1,100 per worker for recordkeeping, notice, or misclassification violations, and up to $5,000 per worker for repeat or willful violations [S2][S3].
Protects workers from being fired or retaliated against for complaining about their classification or filing a related complaint [S2][S3].

Conditions federal unemployment grants on states adopting audits and administrative penalties aimed at employers who misclassify workers to avoid unemployment insurance contributions, and directs targeted Wage and Hour Division audits of industries with frequent misclassification [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies that rely on misclassifying employees as independent contractors would pay: back wages with doubled damages, new civil penalties, and unemployment insurance contributions they currently avoid. Employers that classify correctly would bear only modest recordkeeping and notice costs.

drawbacks.text: The employer presumption backed by clear-and-convincing evidence and per-worker penalties could push some firms to cut contractor work or shift hiring arrangements rather than reclassify, affecting genuine independent contractors and small contracting businesses [S3].

Recordkeeping and notice requirements apply broadly to anyone engaged for labor or services who files an information return, adding compliance costs for businesses of every size, including those that classify correctly [S3].

The unemployment provisions would require state legislation in many states and new state audit programs, an added administrative burden on state agencies and a condition tied to federal grants [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is concrete: workers misclassified as contractors often lose overtime, minimum wage protection, and unemployment coverage, and the bill attacked the practice directly with notice, records, penalties, and a legal presumption in workers' favor. The costs fall almost entirely on firms whose business model depends on the current ambiguity, which is the point of the bill; the compliance burden on firms that classify correctly is real but modest. The main design risk is that per-worker penalties and a strict presumption could push some work arrangements underground or offshore rather than converting them to employee status.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee, got one hearing in June 2010, and then sat there with no committee vote, no floor vote, and no House companion moving, until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Sherrod Brown of Ohio introduced the bill on April 22, 2010, with five Democratic colleagues originally joining him, and it was read twice and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S3][S5].
Eight Senate Democrats total cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
The committee held a hearing on June 17, 2010 (printed as S.Hrg. 111-1146), but never ordered the bill reported or voted on it [S5].
No further action was recorded, and the bill expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that classify workers as independent contractors to avoid overtime, payroll taxes, and unemployment insurance obligations are better off, because the notice, recordkeeping, presumption, and penalty regime never became law and the same fight would have to start over in the next Congress.

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited eight Democratic cosponsors

for.name: Sens. Harkin, Durbin, Murray, Casey, and Merkley
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced

against.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee held a single hearing on the bill but never scheduled a markup or committee vote, leaving it unreported

against.name: Contractor-dependent industries (staffing, construction, trucking, and delivery firms)
against.role: Businesses that rely heavily on independent-contractor classification
against.what_they_did: Opposed misclassification legislation of this type as an attack on the contractor model and its cost advantages

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so the partisan split was never tested; the bill's eight cosponsors were all Democrats, with no Republican support recorded [S4].

industries.industry: Companies using large numbers of independent contractors (staffing, construction, trucking, delivery, janitorial)
industries.note: These firms save on overtime, payroll taxes, and unemployment insurance by classifying workers as contractors; the bill would have made misclassification a violation carrying per-worker penalties and doubled wage damages.

States would have been required to audit employers who misclassify workers to avoid unemployment contributions and to impose administrative penalties, recovering contributions that currently go unpaid; the condition is tied to federal grants.

All firms subject to the wage law would take on recordkeeping for contractors and written classification notices, but compliant firms gain a clearer rule and face less undercutting by competitors who misclassify.
